title: Design a URL Shortener | System Design Interview Short
summary: A classic system design interview question in under a minute: design a URL shortener. The core flow, how to generate short codes, and the one trap interviewers look for.
author: Vinay Mishra
original_value: Answers one interview question in a minute with a clear write path and read path, compares random codes with a counter plus base62, and ends with a three-point answer you can say out loud.
sources: Common system design interview material on URL shorteners (key-value store, base62 encoding, redirect with HTTP 301 or 302)
Base62 uses the characters 0-9, a-z and A-Z; seven characters give 62 to the power 7 combinations, about 3.5 trillion

scenes.headline: Design a URL shortener
scenes.narration: Interviewer says: design a URL shortener. Do not panic. It is just two flows. Let me show you.

scenes.headline: Write and read
items: Write: long URL in, short code out
Store code and URL in a key-value store
Read: code in, look up, redirect
scenes.narration: Write path: take the long URL, make a short code, store the pair. Read path: take the code, look it up, and redirect. Reads are far more common than writes.

scenes.headline: Where is the code from?
scenes.narration: Making the code? Random strings can collide, so you must check the database. Better: a unique counter in base sixty-two. No collisions, and seven characters cover three and a half trillion codes.

scenes.headline: One counter breaks
items: One counter is a single point of failure
Give each server a block of IDs
Cache hot links to protect the database
scenes.narration: The trap: one global counter becomes a bottleneck. Give each server its own block of numbers. And since reads dominate, cache the popular links.

scenes.headline: Your answer
scenes.narration: Your answer: a key-value store, a counter with base sixty-two, and a cache for reads. Follow for the next interview question.
